common_name: Lord Lambourne Miltoniopsis (Historic Pink Pansy Orchid Parent)

planting.note: Repot annually into fresh, fine-grade bark-and-sphagnum mix; Lord Lambourne is one of the historic early Miltonia-type hybrids behind much of modern Miltoniopsis breeding.

directions: One of the classic early Miltonia-type hybrids from the golden age of English orchid breeding, Lord Lambourne bears rounded, flat, soft pink to blush-white flowers with a deeper rose-pink blaze radiating from the throat, held several to a spike above pleated, light-green foliage. It became an influential parent in Miltoniopsis breeding, passing on its clear pink coloring and flat form to countless later pansy-orchid hybrids, including the historic 1925 grex Miltoniopsis Lycaena bred with 'Princess Margaret'. Grow cool, with bright indirect light and evenly moist, fast-draining fine bark mix, since the thin, soft leaves pleat visibly at the first sign of underwatering. Repot annually into fresh medium to avoid the salt buildup that quickly browns leaf tips on this fine-rooted genus.

common_name: Princess Margaret Miltoniopsis (Historic Red-Pink Pansy Orchid Parent)

planting.note: Repot annually into fresh, fine-grade bark-and-sphagnum mix; Princess Margaret is a historic Miltonia-type hybrid from the same early breeding era as 'Lord Lambourne'.

directions: A historic Miltonia-type hybrid from the same early era of English pansy-orchid breeding as 'Lord Lambourne', Princess Margaret carries rounder, deeper rose-red flowers with a more solid wash of color and only a faint pale edge, a step toward the darker reds later Miltoniopsis breeders pursued. Crossed with 'Lord Lambourne' in 1925, it produced the influential grex Miltoniopsis Lycaena, one of the first Miltoniopsis hybrids to approach a nearly solid red flower. Grow cool with bright, indirect light and constant light moisture in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix, since Miltoniopsis roots dry out and die back quickly if allowed to sit bone-dry between waterings. Provide humidity above 60 percent and steady air movement to avoid the fungal spotting that mars flowers in stagnant, poorly ventilated growing areas.

common_name: Eridge Paphiopedilum (Historic Slipper Orchid Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot annually to every other year in fine, fast-draining mix, since Paphiopedilum lacks pseudobulbs for water storage.

directions: One of the primary Paphiopedilum hybrids from the classic Victorian-to-Edwardian era of slipper orchid breeding, Eridge combines mottled foliage with a rounded dorsal sepal and moderate spotting typical of the earliest complex hybrid lines. It is best remembered today as one of the two parents, alongside 'Hampden', behind the historic 1951 grex Paphiopedilum Winston Churchill, still an influential ancestor of modern red-and-white spotted slipper orchids. Grow in bright shade in a fine bark-and-perlite mix kept evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Paphiopedilum has no pseudobulbs to store water through dry spells. Feed lightly and regularly during active growth, since these terrestrial orchids stay continuously rooted and respond poorly to a strict feed-then-flush cycle.

common_name: Hampden Paphiopedilum (Historic Slipper Orchid Parent Hybrid)

planting.note: Repot annually to every other year in fine, fast-draining mix, since Paphiopedilum lacks pseudobulbs for water storage.

directions: A companion primary hybrid to 'Eridge' from the same early period of complex Paphiopedilum breeding, Hampden contributed heavier maroon-red spotting and a broader, more rounded dorsal sepal to its offspring. Combined with 'Eridge' in 1951, it produced the historic grex Paphiopedilum Winston Churchill, whose award-winning cultivar lines still stand behind much of today's standard red-spotted slipper orchid breeding. Grow in bright, filtered shade in a fine, fast-draining bark-and-perlite mix, keeping the root zone evenly moist but never soggy. Because this terrestrial orchid lacks pseudobulbs, avoid letting it dry out fully between waterings, which quickly stresses the plant and stalls flower spike development.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Inspector Morse is a heavily silvered brunnera selection later used to breed 'Mr. Morse'.

directions: Inspector Morse carries heavily silvered, heart-shaped leaves with fine green veining in the classic frosted brunnera style, the silvering developing most fully as clumps mature through their second and third seasons. Crossed with the white-flowered 'Betty Bowring' by a Belgian breeder, it passed on its silvered foliage to the resulting cultivar 'Mr. Morse', which combines both parents' most distinctive traits. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, since both direct sun and dry soil quickly scorch the thin, papery leaves. Divide congested clumps in early spring or right after flowering to maintain vigorous new silver growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Soledad is a mid-twentieth-century diploid daylily grown today chiefly for its breeding history.

directions: Soledad is a mid-twentieth-century daylily best remembered today as one of the two parents, crossed with 'Signal Light', behind Fay-Russell's 1966 Stout Silver Medal winner 'Cartwheels'. Its own blooms come in warm gold tones on well-branched scapes typical of the era's diploid breeding, before tetraploid conversion became widespread in the genus. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, where the dense, grassy clumps bulk up quickly and reward regular division. Split congested clumps every three to four years in spring or immediately after bloom to keep flower counts high.

common_name: Signal Light Daylily (Historic Parent of Cartwheels)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Signal Light is a mid-twentieth-century diploid daylily grown today chiefly for its breeding history.

directions: Paired with 'Soledad' in the cross that produced Fay-Russell's award-winning 'Cartwheels' in 1966, Signal Light is a diploid daylily from the same mid-century breeding era, prized in its day for clear, well-formed blooms held on sturdy scapes above dense, grassy foliage. Grow in average, well-drained soil in full sun, dividing crowded clumps every three to four years to sustain strong bloom counts, since the older diploid habit favors dense multiplication over huge individual flowers. Consistent moisture during bud formation in late spring improves flower size and substance. Once established, it is a reliable, low-maintenance perennial requiring little more than an annual spring cleanup of old foliage.

common_name: Fogbound Bearded Iris (Smoky Violet-Black Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Fogbound is a smoky, near-black Tall Bearded iris later used to breed 'Crystal Gazer'.

directions: Fogbound bears smoky, deep violet-black Tall Bearded iris flowers, the kind of near-black tone that iris breeders spent decades chasing before cultivars this dark became widely available. Crossed with 'Lotus Land' by hybridizer Keith Keppel, it produced the ruffled, lightly laced 'Crystal Gazer', registered in 2002 and honored with an Award of Merit in 2006. Plant rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil, since standing moisture around the rhizome quickly causes rot. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigorous flowering and good air circulation between fans.

common_name: Lotus Land Bearded Iris (Historic Blue-Violet Parent Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Lotus Land is a blue-violet Tall Bearded iris later used to breed 'Crystal Gazer'.

directions: Lotus Land is a Tall Bearded iris grown chiefly today for its role as a parent, crossed with 'Fogbound' by Keith Keppel to produce the acclaimed 'Crystal Gazer' of 2002. Its own flowers show the clean blue-violet tones and good branching typical of the strong Pacific Northwest iris-breeding programs of the era. Set rhizomes shallowly in full sun with the top surface exposed, in well-drained soil that never stays wet for long, since rot quickly sets in around buried or waterlogged rhizomes. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after flowering to keep the planting vigorous and well-aerated.

common_name: Argentina Bearded Iris (Historic Parent of Purissima)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Argentina is an early-twentieth-century Tall Bearded iris grown today chiefly for its breeding history.

directions: Argentina is an early-twentieth-century Tall Bearded iris remembered chiefly as a parent, crossed with 'Conquistador' by hybridizer William Mohr to produce the landmark white iris 'Purissima', named and introduced posthumously by his collaborator W.E. Mitchell in 1927. Grown alongside its era's other historic breeding stock, it stands behind decades of later white and near-white bearded iris cultivars. Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed to full sun in well-drained soil, since standing water quickly rots the fleshy rhizome. Divide every three to four years after bloom to keep clumps vigorous and floriferous.

common_name: Conquistador Bearded Iris (Historic Parent of Purissima)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, with the top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall; Conquistador is an early-twentieth-century Tall Bearded iris grown today chiefly for its breeding history.

directions: Conquistador is the second historic parent, alongside 'Argentina', behind William Mohr's landmark white Tall Bearded iris 'Purissima', introduced in 1927. It is preserved today mainly in historic iris collections for its place in that lineage rather than grown widely as a garden plant on its own merits. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed to full sun in sharply drained soil, since bearded iris rhizomes rot quickly if buried or kept wet. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor and flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted plantlets in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; variegation is brightest with a bit of filtered morning light.

directions: Eco-Butterfly carries the same rounded, olive-green, silver-veined leaves as typical strawberry begonia, but each leaf is broadly edged in creamy white, giving the low mat a distinctly variegated, butterfly-wing pattern. It is the parent selection behind the golden-leaved sport 'Harvest Moon', which replaces the cream variegation with solid sulfur-yellow color. Like the species, it spreads by thin red runners that root at the tip, quickly forming new plantlets that knit into a groundcover under trees or along shaded path edges. Grow in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, since strong sun quickly scorches the thin, variegated leaves and fades the cream edging.

common_name: Queen of Hanover Rex Begonia (Victorian-Era Spiral-Leaved Heirloom)

planting.note: Propagate from rhizome divisions or leaf-wedge cuttings taken in spring, rooting under high humidity at 70-75°F.

directions: Queen of Hanover is a venerable Victorian-era rex begonia grown for its tightly spiraled leaves in olive-green washed with metallic silver, the coiled centers deepening toward the crown and the undersides flushed dark red. It is the parent of the more compact sport 'Princess of Hanover', which carries the same coiling habit in a tighter, smaller spiral. Grow in bright, indirect light with steady warmth and high humidity, since the papery, spiraled leaves scorch quickly in direct sun and stall in cold drafts. Water only once the top inch of the shallow, fast-draining rhizome mix has dried, since rex begonia rhizomes rot readily in soggy soil.
